name: The Local News Collapse
deck: Gannett reported its first positive annual net income since its 2019 merger—and total revenue still fell. That is the structural trap: digital progress is real, print collapse is faster, and no one has cracked a profitable model for covering city hall.
core_bet: Local journalism is not dying because readers stopped caring. It is dying because the classified and small-business advertising that funded newsrooms for 150 years migrated permanently to Google and Meta after 2012. The New York Times proved premium journalism can compound at 12.78M subscribers and $2.825B in revenue—but only because it amortizes costs across a global audience. A newsroom covering Dayton's zoning board cannot do that math. The gap is not a management problem; it is a unit-economics problem that no company in the filings has solved.

mechanism: For 150 years, local newspapers ran on a closed economic loop: display and classified advertising from local businesses funded newsrooms, which produced audience trust, which attracted more advertisers. Digital platforms broke that loop at its highest-margin point. Google absorbed search-linked advertising. Meta absorbed social-display advertising. Craigslist eliminated classified revenues almost entirely. By the mid-2010s, the advertising dollars were gone and the audience had followed distribution to platforms the newspapers did not own.

Gannett's filings show the arithmetic precisely. In Q2 2026, digital revenue was $254.3M—47.4% of total revenue and growing. But total revenue fell 8.3% year-over-year because the legacy print base is contracting faster than digital replaces it. The company generated $45.6M in digital-only subscription revenue in that quarter, which is real money—except it has to fund newsrooms in hundreds of local markets simultaneously. The per-market economics do not work.

Local broadcast television had a temporary reprieve through retransmission fees. Cable and satellite operators pay local stations to carry their signals, creating a distribution revenue stream that has nothing to do with the value of local journalism. Nexstar's distribution revenue—$2.924B in FY2025—now exceeds its advertising revenue of $1.959B by nearly 50%. But retransmission fees are under their own pressure as broadband replaces cable, and they fund distribution infrastructure, not reporting. When political advertising collapsed in Q4 2025—dropping $233M in a single quarter to just $21M—Nexstar posted a net loss of $(170)M despite collecting $720M in distribution fees that quarter.

The New York Times shows what sustainable journalism economics looks like: $1.951B in subscription revenue, 12.78M total subscribers at year-end 2025, and $9.94 monthly digital ARPU by Q2 2026. The company can charge that because it owns direct billing relationships with subscribers in every ZIP code in the country—and because Games, Cooking, The Athletic, and Wirecutter spread the cost of the newsroom across multiple daily habits. No local newspaper has those product lines. The Dayton Daily News cannot sell a Wordle subscription to offset the cost of a reporter at city hall.
why_now: The inflection was not a single event but a compressing timeline that became unambiguous by 2025. Gannett's 2019 merger with GateHouse Media was a direct bet that scale could solve what individual papers could not—consolidate costs, share back-office functions, convert a larger audience into digital subscriptions. Six years later, FY2025 produced the first positive annual net income since that merger, and yet total revenue was still declining. That means the consolidation strategy bought time but did not change the unit economics. Meanwhile, Nexstar's Q4 2025 results crystallized the broadcast version of the same problem: when political advertising ended, the quarter that had looked viable on distribution fees collapsed to a $(170)M net loss. Both data points arrived in the same reporting cycle, both pointing at the same gap: there is no profitable model for local accountability journalism at scale, and the companies closest to solving it are still losing the race against their own legacy declines.
who_pays: Residents of any city or county that has lost its newspaper beat reporters pay through civic blindness. Without someone in the county courthouse, planning-board meetings produce no public record. Without reporters covering school-board budgets, administrators cut programs without scrutiny. Without a local health reporter, a contamination story or hospital-staffing crisis goes unreported for months. The cost does not appear on anyone's balance sheet, but it compounds: misallocated public money, unchecked institutional malfeasance, lower voter turnout in local elections where the decisions closest to daily life actually get made.
who_profits: Google and Meta absorbed the advertising dollars that once funded newsrooms. They did not replace the journalism; they replaced the advertising product that paid for it. The New York Times, by contrast, captured the premium end of the remaining subscriber market—$1.951B in subscription revenue in FY2025 proves the model works nationally. Nexstar collects retransmission fees from cable and satellite subscribers even as it cuts newsroom headcount; the distribution infrastructure extracts value from the local-news brand without funding the reporting that built it.
tension: The companies in the filings that are closest to solving the local-news problem are demonstrating that it is not yet solved. Gannett is executing a credible digital transition—digital is nearly half of revenue, digital-only subscriptions outnumber print subscribers, and the company posted its first positive net income since its 2019 merger. And total revenue still fell 8.3% in Q2 2026. Nexstar owns more local TV stations than any other company in the U.S. and still depends on cable retransmission fees—not journalism value—to stay solvent. The New York Times proves the subscription model works, but only at national scale with a product bundle (Games, Cooking, The Athletic, Wirecutter) that local papers cannot replicate. The gap is structural: the audience for local accountability journalism exists, but it will not pay $20 per month for city-hall coverage, and no advertiser will fill the shortfall.
surprising_part: Nexstar's distribution revenue in FY2025 was $2.924B—nearly $1B more than its $1.959B advertising revenue. That means the money keeping local TV stations alive is not coming from viewers or advertisers who value local journalism. It is coming from the cable bundle as a legacy contractual obligation. Cable operators pay to carry local stations because federal must-carry rules and retransmission negotiations force them to, not because local news commands premium value. When cord-cutting eliminates the cable bundle—Comcast ended 2025 with 11.270M video customers, down from prior years—that revenue stream disappears too. The local TV model is not surviving on journalism economics; it is surviving on regulatory and contractual inertia that is itself eroding.
one_sentence: Gannett posted its first profit since its 2019 merger while total revenue kept falling—and that is the most honest single data point about where local journalism stands: digital progress is real, structural collapse is faster, and no company has built a profitable model for covering city hall.
societal_stake: Democratic accountability at the local level requires that someone is watching—and for 150 years, that someone was funded by local advertisers who needed the newspaper as much as the newspaper needed them. That arrangement is over. The companies that absorbed the advertising dollars (Google, Meta) have no civic obligation and no economic reason to rebuild local reporting. The companies that still own local media (Gannett, Nexstar) are fighting structural arithmetic. Communities where newspapers have closed or shrunk dramatically have documented higher municipal borrowing costs, lower voter turnout, and less public scrutiny of local officials. The collapse is not a media-industry problem; it is a governance problem wearing a media-industry face.

evidence.fact: FY2025 total revenue $2.302B; first positive net income since 2019 merger ($1.7M net income attributable to USA TODAY Co.); digital revenue 46% of total (~$1.1B); digital-only subscriptions reached 1.5M by end of 2025, outnumbering print subscriptions; Q2 2026 total revenue $536.3M down 8.3% year-over-year despite digital revenue of $254.3M (47.4% of total); digital-only subscription revenue $45.6M in Q2 2026; adjusted EBITDA $56.9M in Q2 2026

FY2025 total revenue $2.825B; subscription revenue $1.951B; total subscribers 12.78M at end of FY2025; digital-only subscribers 12.80M in Q2 2026; digital-only ARPU $9.94 in Q2 2026; digital advertising revenue +20.7% in Q2 2026; full-year 2025 free cash flow $550.5M; demonstrates profitable subscription model only achievable with national scale and multi-product bundle

FY2025 net revenue $4.949B; distribution revenue $2.924B vs advertising revenue $1.959B—distribution exceeds advertising by nearly 50%; Q4 2025 net loss $(170)M as political advertising fell $233M to $21M; Q1 2026 net income recovery to $160M; Q2 2026 net revenue $1.993B including $1.116B distribution revenue vs $862M advertising; business model depends on cable retransmission fees, not on the value of local journalism

Video subscribers declined to 11.270M by end of 2025; announced intent to separate NBCUniversal and Sky in Q2 2026; structural shift away from cable-and-content bundle is accelerating, removing the cord-bundle infrastructure that funds local retransmission fees

Pay-TV subscribers 6.391M in Q2 2026, down from 6.632M in Q1 2026; pay-TV segment substantially deconsolidated as of June 2026; going-concern uncertainty raised in FY2025 annual report; satellite TV infrastructure for local-channel delivery deteriorating
